entries.title: Spoofed update server
entries.description: Fake backend delivers a malicious update to the TCU.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker impersonates the OEM update server (DNS or rogue base-station redirection) and serves a manifest and package.
entries.damage_scenario: Malicious firmware is installed, giving control of the TCU and gateway functions.
entries.rationale: Requires redirecting cellular traffic and some knowledge of the update protocol; impact is severe because the TCU bridges to vehicle networks.
assumptions: TLS server certificate validation is the only server authentication in the baseline design.
alternatives: Accept risk only if manifest signatures are verified independently of TLS (see CR-016).

entries.title: Man-in-the-middle on update download
entries.description: Update traffic is intercepted and modified between the backend and the TCU.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker operates a rogue cellular base station or compromised network element and alters or replays the package in transit.
entries.damage_scenario: Tampered or outdated package reaches the OTA client; availability of updates degraded.
entries.rationale: Needs specialised radio equipment and expertise, which lowers feasibility compared with simple spoofing.

entries.title: Tampered OTA update package
entries.description: Attacker modifies the firmware image in transit or at the backend.
entries.attack_vector: Firmware image is altered in the update pipeline, in transit, or in storage before the OTA client verifies it.
entries.damage_scenario: Unauthorised code executes on the TCU with access to vehicle network gateways.
entries.rationale: Pipeline access or transit interception is plausible for a capable attacker; integrity protection must not depend on the channel alone.
assumptions: The package is verified on the TCU before being written to the inactive partition.
alternatives: Add a second signature check at activation (secure boot) if verification happens only at download time.

entries.title: Manipulated update manifest
entries.description: Manifest metadata (version, hash, expiry) is altered to force a freeze or mix-and-match attack.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker alters or replays manifest fields so that incompatible or stale components are installed or updates are withheld.
entries.damage_scenario: TCU stays on vulnerable firmware or ends in an inconsistent software state.
entries.rationale: Needs protocol knowledge and a position on the update path; effect is limited unless combined with other attacks.

entries.title: Denial of update service
entries.description: Updates are blocked or repeatedly interrupted so that fixes cannot be delivered.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker floods the update endpoint or interrupts the cellular link during download or installation.
entries.damage_scenario: Vehicles remain unpatched or an interrupted installation leaves the TCU unavailable.
entries.rationale: Jamming and flooding need little expertise; impact is limited to availability of the update function.

entries.title: Compromise of the update-signing key
entries.description: Backend signing key is stolen and used to sign malicious packages.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker breaches the backend signing environment or insider misuses the signing key.
entries.damage_scenario: Fleet-wide malicious update with valid signatures.
entries.rationale: Requires deep access to a protected signing environment; feasibility is very low but impact is fleet-wide.

entries.title: Unauthorized diagnostic session
entries.description: Attacker opens a privileged diagnostic session through the OBD-II port.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker connects a tester to the OBD-II connector and brute-forces or bypasses UDS security access.
entries.damage_scenario: Privileged diagnostic services become available, enabling data read-out or reprogramming.
entries.rationale: Physical access is needed but OBD-II is widely reachable; weak seed-key schemes lower the effort.

entries.title: Unauthorized firmware flashing via UDS
entries.description: UDS download services are used to write attacker firmware.
entries.attack_vector: RequestDownload and TransferData services are invoked after a weak or bypassed security access.
entries.damage_scenario: Attacker firmware runs on the TCU.
entries.rationale: Secure boot raises the effort significantly, so feasibility is rated low.

entries.title: Sensitive data read via diagnostic identifiers
entries.description: Personal or secret data is read out by data identifier.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker reads location history, VIN-linked data or configuration values through ReadDataByIdentifier.
entries.damage_scenario: Privacy breach and exposure of configuration useful for later attacks.
entries.rationale: Low effort when identifiers are not access-controlled per session level.

entries.title: Diagnostic interface fuzzing and denial of service
entries.description: Malformed diagnostic requests crash or lock the diagnostic stack.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker sends malformed UDS or DoIP frames at high rate through the OBD-II connector.
entries.damage_scenario: Diagnostic stack or TCU services become unavailable.
entries.rationale: Fuzzing tools are public and need little expertise.

entries.title: CAN message injection
entries.description: Forged CAN frames are injected to manipulate vehicle functions.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker with bus access (directly or via a compromised node) injects frames using valid identifiers.
entries.damage_scenario: Unintended vehicle behaviour such as false speed, torque or door-lock states.
entries.rationale: Unauthenticated frames are accepted by receivers; bus access requires a foothold.
assumptions: Body CAN frames carry no authentication in the current design.
alternatives: Isolate Body CAN by gateway filtering if message authentication cannot be added.

entries.title: Replay of CAN messages
entries.description: Previously recorded valid CAN frames are replayed.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker records legitimate frames and retransmits them at a chosen time.
entries.damage_scenario: Stale commands (for example remote lock) are accepted as current.
entries.rationale: Recording and replay tools are simple; success depends on the lack of freshness values.

entries.title: CAN bus flooding
entries.description: High-priority frames saturate the bus.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker transmits frames with low identifiers continuously, starving legitimate traffic.
entries.damage_scenario: Loss of cyclic signals and degraded functions.
entries.rationale: Trivial to execute once bus access is gained.

entries.title: Rogue device or spoofed SOME/IP service
entries.description: A rogue node offers or consumes SOME/IP services.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker connects a device to the Ethernet network or compromises a node and announces forged service offers.
entries.damage_scenario: Malicious data reaches consumers such as the head unit or ADAS controller.
entries.rationale: Without port authentication any connected device can join the VLAN.

entries.title: Eavesdropping on inter-domain Ethernet traffic
entries.description: Unencrypted service traffic is captured.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker taps the link or mirrors a switch port and records SOME/IP payloads such as location data.
entries.damage_scenario: Disclosure of location and state information.
entries.rationale: Requires physical or switch access; consequence limited to confidentiality.

entries.title: VLAN hopping or switch misconfiguration
entries.description: Traffic crosses VLAN boundaries.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker exploits double tagging or a misconfigured trunk to reach protected segments.
entries.damage_scenario: Access to segregated domains.
entries.rationale: Requires a foothold and knowledge of switch configuration.

entries.title: Theft of device credentials for backend access
entries.description: Device certificate and key are copied and reused.
entries.attack_vector: Credentials are extracted from storage or memory and used to impersonate the device towards the backend.
entries.damage_scenario: Impersonation of vehicles, fraudulent data upload and remote command abuse.
entries.rationale: Needs access to credential storage; HSM-backed storage raises the effort.

entries.title: Exposure of telematics data
entries.description: Location and trip data is exposed in transit or at rest.
entries.attack_vector: Data is intercepted, or backend access control is bypassed to read stored telematics data.
entries.damage_scenario: Privacy breach affecting vehicle owners.
entries.rationale: Personal data is a high-value target; protection depends on both channel and backend controls.

entries.title: Forged remote command
entries.description: A remote lock or climate command is injected into the TCU command channel.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker hijacks a backend session or replays a command message.
entries.damage_scenario: Unauthorised vehicle access (unlocking) or unsafe activation.
entries.rationale: Needs backend session compromise or credential theft.

entries.title: Key material extraction
entries.description: Device keys are extracted from the hardware.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker with physical access uses probing, fault injection or debug access to read secrets from the device.
entries.damage_scenario: Cloned device identity and ability to forge signed data.
entries.rationale: Requires specialised equipment and expertise; HSM usage raises effort.

entries.title: Debug interface abuse (JTAG / UART)
entries.description: Debug ports are used to dump or modify firmware.
entries.attack_vector: Attacker connects to an enabled JTAG or UART port and reads memory or halts the processor.
entries.damage_scenario: Firmware disclosure and bypass of software protections.
entries.rationale: Debug ports are well known; production lock-down determines feasibility.
assumptions: Debug ports are open on development hardware; production lock-down is still under review.
alternatives: Permanently disable debug in production fuses.
